<reason>A built a consistent, disciplined case: the motion targets consenting adults altering their own bodies, so PRO's strongest harms (embryos, grandchildren, intergenerational effects) all belong to germline editing, which is already regulated separately and thus outside the scope A had to defend. A pressed this scope point from the opening through the closing, used clean analogies (rhinoplasty, braces, drug licensing, doping/medical-tourism displacement) to argue regulation beats prohibition, and answered B's pressure questions with a properly formatted A1/A2 that landed a genuine reductio: if unverifiability justifies banning recreational somatic enhancement, it equally justifies banning somatic gene therapy for disease, which even PRO wouldn't accept. B never rebutted this reductio in Rebuttal 2 or Closing, instead repeating that the somatic/germline "wall" is unenforceable without addressing that a ban suffers the identical verification problem, plus pushes the practice underground with zero registries. B's collective-action-trap and pleiotropy arguments were vivid and original, but by the end they mostly restated the "no X-ray vision into cells" framing rather than closing the gap A exposed. Both sides suffered a clipped turn (B's opening, A's Rebuttal 2), a roughly symmetric execution cost that does not change the outcome. A's tighter framing, sharper direct engagement with pressure questions, and the unanswered reductio give it the clearer, more resolved path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 point that PRO's unverifiability argument, if valid, would equally ban somatic gene therapy for disease (which PRO does not accept) went unanswered through B's Closing, decisively undercutting PRO's core enforcement argument.</best_rebuttal>
